Founded in 1874, the brand pairs an avant-garde approach to design with an uncompromising understanding of fine watchmaking and high luxury. Introduced in 1979, the Polo is arguably Piaget’s most recognizable creation and one of the purest expressions of the luxury sports watch. Originally conceived with quartz movements and crafted almost exclusively in 18K gold, it emerged as Piaget’s answer to contemporaries such as the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak and Patek Philippe Nautilus, though executed with an unmistakably glamorous identity all its own. The ref. 15562 C 701 captures the original Polo concept at its most quintessential. Its rounded 18K yellow-gold case flows seamlessly into the integrated bracelet, while the matching gold dial continues the bracelet’s alternating brushed and polished horizontal gadroons directly across the watch’s face. Discreet day and date displays add everyday practicality without disrupting the design’s remarkable continuity. Remaining unpolished, this example retains the richly defined surfaces and sculptural proportions that make the early Polo so compelling. Worn less like a conventional wristwatch and more like a custom-crafted piece of jewelry, it is a distinctly Piaget expression of effortless 1980s opulence. Sourced directly from the family of its original owner, it presents a rare opportunity to acquire an early Polo with a remarkably limited ownership history, something that can seldom be said of a model whose examples have typically traded hands many times over. title: 1990s Precista Royal Navy Diver (6645-99-757-3314) “Sterile Case Back”
description: Precista occupies an interesting and often overlooked position in the history of British military watches. Originally associated with the British watch and clock supplier Southern Watch & Clock Supplies Ltd., the company was among a relatively small group of manufacturers that produced watches for the British Ministry of Defense, including general-service watches and purpose-built divers for the Royal Navy. While Precista's military diving watches can be traced back to the early 1980s, the present watch belongs to the later generation of quartz-powered divers produced during the late 1980s and early 1990s. These watches followed the utilitarian requirements that had come to define the British military dive watch: a stainless-steel case with fixed strap bars, screw-down crown, rotating timing bezel, highly legible matte-black dial, and tritium luminous material identified by the circled "T" prominently displayed on the dial. There was little here that wasn't dictated by function. The present example carries NATO Stock Number 6645-99-757-3314 , an NSN associated with British military quartz diving watches and found on documented Royal Navy-issued Precista examples from the period. Unlike many surviving examples, however, this watch is unusual in that its case back carries the NATO Stock Number without the individual issue and year markings normally found beneath it. Issued examples are typically encountered with a sequential number followed by the year of issue, for example, documented Precista divers from 1988, 1989, and 1993 are known with this NSN and corresponding military issue numbers. Collectors commonly refer to examples such as the present watch, which lack these individual issue markings, as having a "sterile" case back . Precisely why these sterile examples exist is less clear. They may represent unissued contract watches, replacement or service stock, or watches that otherwise remained outside the normal individual-issue marking process. Without surviving documentation connecting this particular watch to one of those scenarios, however, we prefer not to speculate beyond what can be established from the watch itself. What remains is an exceptionally well-preserved example of a lesser-known British military diver of the period. Its matte-black 3-6-9 dial, oversized circled "T," sword-shaped hands, fully graduated bezel, fixed bars, and bead-blasted case give it an unmistakably military character, while its scarcity relative to the considerably better-known CWC divers makes the Precista a fascinating component of the post-MilSub Royal Navy dive-watch story. title: 1984 Rolex GMT-Master (Ref. 16750)
description: The Rolex GMT-Master, a symbol of sophistication and versatility, has a storied history that dates back to 1954. It all started when Rolex received a request from Pan American Airways (Pan Am) to develop a technical pilot's watch capable of displaying two time zones simultaneously. With the advent of commercial transcontinental flights, Pan Am needed a watch for their long-haul international flight crews that would enable them to keep track of time in multiple locations. GMT, which stands for Greenwich Mean Time, is the universal time standard that regulates the world's clocks and serves as the basis for aviation planning and schedules. The Rolex GMT-Master is equipped with a fourth 24-hour hand that displays the same time zone as the standard 12-hour hand but on a 24-hour scale. This GMT hand allows wearers to set the watch to GMT or any other time zone and then adjust the offset using the rotating 24-hour bezel to display a second timezone. This remarkable feature makes the Rolex GMT-Master a must-have for anyone who frequently travels across multiple time zones, allowing them to easily and precisely track two time zones. The Rolex ref. 16750 was the third GMT-Master model introduced by the Crown and was the direct successor to the long-running model, the ref. 1675. First introduced in 1979 and discontinued in 1988, the ref. 16750 only had a short window of production compared to its constituents, especially considering the very transitional nature of the reference. The most notable upgrade initially introduced with the GMT-Master ref. 16750 was the employment of the cal. 3035 quickset movement, a first for the GMT at the time. Due to the very transitional nature of this ref. 16750, the 9-year production window is broken into two dial variations, the early matte dial version, and the later glossy dial version. title: 1960s Lemania "RAN" HS9 Mono-Pusher Chronograph (Royal Australian Navy) Series II
description: Military-issued chronographs represent one of the most compelling corners of vintage watch collecting, combining purpose-built design with tangible historical provenance. Among them, the single-pusher chronographs produced by Lemania are particularly significant. Better known as one of Switzerland’s great chronograph movement manufacturers, supplying calibers to brands including Omega, Heuer, and Tissot, Lemania also produced a comparatively small number of watches under its own name, including specialized chronographs supplied to military forces around the world. Lemania’s military mono-pusher chronographs were produced from the 1940s through the early 1970s and supplied most famously to Britain’s Royal Air Force and Fleet Air Arm, as well as to armed forces in Australia, Sweden, and South Africa. Collectors generally divide these watches into three generations according to their case construction: Series I with external caseback notches, Series II with internal notches, and the later Series III distinguished by its asymmetrical case. This example belongs to the particularly scarce Series II and was produced for the Royal Australian Navy, identified by the prominent “RAN” signature replacing the customary Lemania branding on the dial. Produced specifically for the RAN’s Hydrographic Service under the HS9 designation, these watches were issued in remarkably small numbers, with only a fraction of surviving examples displaying this distinctive RAN-signed dial. The watch retains the utilitarian character expected of a purpose-built military instrument, with a highly legible white dial, oversized Arabic numerals, luminous hands and hour plots, twin registers, and the military Broad Arrow prominently displayed above six o’clock. The dial is additionally signed “INCABLOC,” despite the movement itself not utilizing an Incabloc shock-protection system, a curious but known and documented discrepancy found on these RAN examples. Combining the mechanical appeal of Lemania’s celebrated single-pusher chronograph architecture with an exceptionally uncommon Royal Australian Navy configuration, this Series II HS9 represents a fascinating and seldom-seen chapter in both Lemania and Commonwealth military watch history. If it weren't for the Nautilus or Grand Complications series, Patek Philippe would undoubtedly be best known for the Calatrava. The Patek Philippe Calatrava is the truest representation of the classic dress watch, and was first introduced to the world in 1932 with the model reference 92. The sleek, round cases of the Calatrava often feature extremely simple, yet perfectly executed designs with elegant dials that lack all unnecessary obstructions. A true "must-have" for any Patek collector or dress watch aficionado. While there are nearly countless options and iterations of Patek's classic dress watch line, we love the Calatrava ref. 5000R for its modern take on the classic platform. The limited edition model was produced in a run of 5000 pieces, only 500 of which were created in white gold. It is also believed that the ref. 5000R was created in collaboration with Ferrari to create a watch with a dial that emulates the design of the dials used in vintage Ferrari dashboard gauges, which is why this Calatrava has a deep contrast and unique utilitarian styling to the dial. While Patek Philippe has produced countless variations of its iconic Calatrava, the ref. 5000R stands out for its contemporary interpretation of the classic dress watch. Produced in a limited run of approximately 1,700–2,000 examples, with only 100-250 cased in rose gold. The model is perhaps best known for its rumored, though never officially confirmed, connection to Ferrari, as many examples feature a black sector-style dial believed to have been inspired by the instrumentation found in vintage Ferrari dashboard gauges. However, the reference was offered with several dial color configurations, including this exceptionally desirable pink-on-pink execution. Beyond its extremely limited production, the true appeal of the ref. 5000R lies in its coveted "pink-on-pink" configuration, a warm rose gold case paired with a matching pink dial. Pink-on-pink Patek Philippe references have long been among the most sought-after executions in the brand's history, tracing their desirability back to rare vintage Calatravas and perpetual calendars. Their combination of rarity, warmth, and understated elegance has made them enduring favorites among collectors, with that appreciation naturally carrying into Patek's neo-vintage era. The ref. 5000R perfectly captures that legacy, offering one of the most refined and visually harmonious executions of the neo-vintage Calatrava. description: Founded in 1972, Cabot Watch Company (CWC) was established with the goal of producing purpose-built military timepieces for the British Ministry of Defense. Over the following decades, the company became one of the MOD's principal suppliers, manufacturing wristwatches for a variety of British military branches and earning a reputation for rugged, no-nonsense tool watches designed for operational use. In 1980, CWC was awarded the contract to replace the legendary Rolex-issued Royal Navy Submariner, commonly referred to today as the "MilSub." The first generation of CWC Royal Navy divers featured an automatic movement, a dial inspired by the Omega Seamaster 300, and an acrylic bezel insert. In 1983, the specification evolved to a quartz movement, improving reliability and reducing maintenance while retaining the proven Monnin-style case design closely associated with the Heuer Ref. 844 and other professional dive watches of the era. Quartz Royal Navy divers remained in military service for nearly two decades before being gradually superseded by the CWC SBS diver in the early 2000s. Today, these issued Royal Navy watches are recognized as some of the most historically significant British military wristwatches of the modern era, combining authentic military provenance with relatively low production numbers and an unmistakably utilitarian aesthetic. This example from 1995 was produced as part of the continued evolution of CWC's Royal Navy dive watch program, the 1995 specification features the updated CWC signed dial with an enlarged circled "T," "QUARTZ" designation, and the reliable ETA 955.122 quartz movement housed within the rugged M.R.P. S.A. manufactured Monnin style case, a design shared with several iconic professional dive watches of the era, including the Heuer Ref. 844. Today, the CWC Royal Navy Quartz Diver occupies an important place in British military watch collecting. Issued to the Royal Navy throughout the 1980s and 1990s, these watches represent the culmination of the Ministry of Defense's quartz dive watch program before eventually being superseded by the CWC SBS Diver. Their documented military provenance, purpose-built design, and comparatively limited production have made them increasingly sought after by collectors of issued military timepieces. title: 1983 Rolex Air-King (Ref. 5500) "Domino's Pizza"
description: 1983 was an exciting year. Return of the Jedi captivated audiences worldwide, Michael Jackson released Thriller, and Sally Ride became the first American woman to travel to space. At the same time, Domino's Pizza was one of the most prominent fast-food pizza franchises in America. This eccentric Rolex Air-King was the ultimate trophy for one successful Domino's Pizza franchise owner who had to achieve back-to-back weeks of exceptional sales figures. Rolex watches with dials that were co-branded with the logos of corporations and organizations were seen in a variety of different references. However, none are as popular or iconic as the Air-Kings that featured logo dials. The Air-King was the preferred choice for co-branding thanks to the watch's price point and availability, and since these watches were generally being purchased and printed with the intent of being given to employees as awards or gifts, it made sense to use a budget-minded model. After all, a free Rolex is a free Rolex! That being said, the most notorious amongst the co-branded logo dials is, without a doubt, the Domino's Pizza Air-King. There is something magically absurd about the juxtaposition of the idealized totem of luxury that is a Rolex watch and the bold, unmistakable logo of an iconic fast-food pizza chain. It’s something that makes these watches irresistible to many, especially when you add the nostalgia factor and the incredibly fond memories many of us have for the "30 minutes or less" pizza chain, and this has all culminated in a collecting frenzy when it comes to the Domino’s Air-Kings. As the story goes, Tom Monaghan opened the first Domino's Pizza location in 1960 in Michigan and quickly expanded to the surrounding areas after seeing early success. Thanks to the franchise model the brand adopted early on, Domino's Pizza opened its 1000th store 23 years later. Monaghan replied, "Turn in a $20,000 sales week, and it's yours!" Apart from that lone Bulova and a few Seikos, which were given out as awards, Domino's Pizza quickly landed on the Rolex Air-King as the company's premier award prize. At first, a franchise owner only had to have a $20,000 sales week, and the Rolex was theirs, but due to the exponential growth in popularity Domino's enjoyed at the time, that sales goal was increased to $25,000 a week for 4 weeks in a row. Rolex signified its more economical timepieces with the text "Precision" printed on the dial. These watches carried in-house movements that were well-made but manually wound. This was until the Air-King was introduced to the world in 1957, and it became the premier model of Rolex’s more affordable Precision model range. title: Tropical 1948 Longines Sei-Tacche (Ref. 23788) Military Dial
description: Longines is one of the oldest continuously operating watch manufacturers in the world, with roots dating back to 1832. Over that immense period of time, the brand has crafted some truly incredible and incredibly accurate timepieces. In fact, it's one of the reasons Longines is the official timekeeper of the Kentucky Derby, where accuracy is paramount. Among vintage Longines, few models capture the imagination of collectors quite like the “Sei-Tacche.” Produced in the 1930s and 1940s alongside the earlier “Tre-Tacche,” these watches earned their names from their distinctive casebacks, six notches for the Sei-Tacche, three for the Tre-Tacche, engineered for a tighter seal and requiring specialized tools to remove. Beyond this functional innovation, the Sei-Tacche has become a cult favorite, celebrated for its uncompromising simplicity and its place as one of the earliest true “tool watches” before the category even had a name. This 1951 example ref. 23788 brings all the hallmarks that collectors seek: a 33mm stainless steel case, a warm military-style dial with bold radium-lumed Arabic numerals, a red 24-hour scale for a touch of color, and a refined blue steel handset. The six-notched caseback and rugged construction speak to Longines’ wartime focus on reliability and resilience, making these pieces both historically significant and incredibly wearable today. For collectors, the Sei-Tacche represents more than just a vintage Longines; it embodies the brand’s legacy of precision and durability, qualities that established its reputation in both civilian and military circles. With its understated aesthetics, robust build, and undeniable historical importance, the Sei-Tacche remains one of the most compelling entry points into serious vintage Longines collecting. title: 1982 Rolex Day-Date 18K WG (Ref. 18039) Onyx Stone Dial
description: In 1977, Rolex introduced the Day-Date reference 18039, ushering in a new era for the iconic “President” line through a series of meaningful technical refinements. Most notably, the reference debuted the sapphire crystal and the upgraded Cal. 3055 movement, which introduced the convenience of a quick-set date function via the second crown position. This advancement earned the reference the nickname “Single-Quick” Day-Date and marked a significant evolution in both functionality and modernity for Rolex’s flagship dress watch. On an extremely limited basis, Rolex produced timepieces featuring exotic materials, crafting dials from a wide array of minerals, woods, and stones such as black onyx, burl wood, lapis lazuli, birch, fossil, coral, aventurine, and ferrite, among others. Each exotic variant was strikingly vivid in appearance while maintaining a minimalist elegance, and production numbers varied greatly depending on the rarity and difficulty of sourcing the material itself; the rarer the material, the fewer examples Rolex produced. Today, well-preserved examples of these exotic Rolex Day-Date references have become exponentially harder to find, fueled by a devoted cult following and limited market circulation, as collectors rarely part with them due to the individuality, artistry, and coveted value each unique dial retains. As a result, whenever one surfaces for sale, it is regarded as something truly special. On an even more exclusive, perhaps even finite, basis, Rolex fitted these exotic stone dials into white metal references such as 18K white gold and platinum. Regarded by many collectors as the ultimate “holy grails” of stone dial collecting, some of these production runs are believed to consist of only a handful of examples. These exceptionally elusive, near-mythical executions transform the character of the stone dial entirely, pairing the organic depth of the material with the cool, restrained elegance of white metal to create a sharper, more refined aesthetic rarely seen within Rolex’s traditionally warm-toned luxury pedigree. This particular example, fitted with its original black onyx stone dial, represents one of the most desirable configurations within the entire stone dial Day-Date lineage. Preserved in remarkable collector-worthy condition, the watch retains a flawless dial and an impressively strong case, further elevated by its proximity in serial sequence to another known example previously sold through Phillips in 2017. The cool restraint of white gold paired against the deep, uninterrupted black surface of the onyx creates a uniquely sharp and sophisticated aesthetic, one far more understated and architectural than its yellow gold counterparts, while remaining unmistakably luxurious, underscoring both the rarity and significance of this extraordinary reference. title: 1995 Rolex Day-Date 18K WG (Ref. 18239) Sapphire "Teardrop" Dial
description: The Rolex Day-Date is one of the most iconic and beautiful watches in the Rolex catalog. The Rolex Day-Date earned the nickname "President" after it was rumored that President Dwight Eisenhower wore one, but Eisenhower actually wore a Rolex 18K yellow gold Oyster-Perpetual Datejust, which Rolex gifted to him in 1953. However, the nickname "President" is quite fitting for the Day-Date, as Presidents Kennedy, Johnson, Ford, Reagan, Nixon, and Roosevelt all wore the Rolex Day-Date. Apart from its executive affiliation, the Day-Date is a symbol of status and luxury, only produced in highly refined precious metals, including 18K yellow, white, and rose gold, and also platinum, featuring both the day and date complications within the movement. Rolex introduced the cal. 3155 in 1988, this movement featured an updated double-quickset complication, allowing the user to set both the day and date complications quickly. While in position two of the crown, rotating the crown clockwise will promptly change the date, while counterclockwise will quickly change the day. Rolex consistently strikes the perfect balance between luxury and functionality, and this end-of-series 18K white gold Day-Date ref. 18239 from 1995 exemplifies that harmony. Featuring a rare sapphire “teardrop” dial, it stands as a fitting testament to the brand’s enduring commitment to quality. title: 1983 Rolex Daytona (Ref. 6263) Silver "Big Red" Dial
description: Rolex first introduced the Cosmograph in 1963 in steel, 14k, and 18k yellow gold with a design that was solely focused on automobile racing. The Units Per Hour bezel allowed for the tracking and measuring of average speed and lap times, making for a truly useful tool for racing drivers in the 20th century. Rolex, being the same marketing powerhouse back then as they are today, knew the American market would be their most effective demographic as racing in America was on the rise in the 60s-70s. Effectively, in 1964, the Rolex Cosmograph was branded “Daytona” after the famous race, the 24 Hours of Daytona, and the rest is history. The Daytona saw its first major update in late 1969 when Rolex decided to bring its Oyster technology to the Cosmograph. Accompanying the "Oyster" text on the dial, the case crown was upgraded to a 7mm trip-lock crown, and the most significant upgrade was the introduction of the screw-down chronograph pushers, which is a function we still see today in the modern Daytona offering from Rolex. While the case size of this new model was the same as its predecessor at 36mm, the larger crown and more robust pushers greatly increase the watch's wrist presence. The svelte stainless steel Oyster case serves as the perfect counterbalance—restrained, purposeful, and wholly timeless. description: The art of collecting military-issued timepieces has never been more interesting or captivating than in today’s day and age. The “Armée de Terre” dive watch created by J. Bianchi for the French Armies Recon Dive Units is an embodiment of the uncompromising spirit of France’s elite reconnaissance units. Born from the legacy of military tool watches issued throughout the 20th century, the Armée de Terre was designed to meet the rigorous demands of field operatives—both past and present. Originally commissioned by the French Army in the early 1990s for its combat diving units. Developed in collaboration with the Centre École de Plongée de l’Armée de Terre (CEPAT), this watch was designed to meet the rigorous demands of specialized units such as the SAF (spécialistes d'aide au franchissement) and TSIO (travaux subaquatiques/intervention offensive), who operated in challenging environments like rivers, lakes, and urban waterways. Jacques Bianchi, a renowned Marseille-based watchmaker, was awarded the contract after his prototypes outperformed competitors in field tests. The watch's design emphasizes functionality: a 42mm stainless steel case with a satin finish to reduce reflections, an oversized, serrated bezel for ease of use with gloves, and a dial featuring large tritium-lumed markers for optimal visibility. Powered by the reliable ETA 2824 automatic movement, the watch also includes a unidirectional 60-click bezel and a flat mineral glass crystal for enhanced durability. Between 1993 and 1994, approximately 1,000 units were produced and issued exclusively to army divers. These watches were not sold to the public and were intended to be returned and reissued within the military upon personnel transfers, making them exceedingly rare in civilian hands today. Each watch was registered within its respective diving unit, and due to decentralized record-keeping, tracing individual histories is basically impossible. Notably, these timepieces were also designed to be mounted on underwater navigation boards, underscoring their role as essential tools for military operations. The J. Bianchi “Armée de Terre” diver watch stands as a testament to military engineering and horological craftsmanship, with the few models that surface offering a genuine piece of French military history. description: First introduced in 1963 the Rolex Daytona has remained a sought-after stable within the Rolex product range. Designed with professional racecar drivers in mind, the Daytona’s precision chronograph and tachymeter bezel allowed drivers to accurately measure speeds up to 400 kilometers or miles per hour. The release of the Daytona came just after Rolex had become the official timekeeper of the Daytona racetrack and the name evolved as a way for the brand to highlight its connection to the celebrated race. Early Daytona models featured a manual-wind Valjoux 72-based column-wheel chronograph movement. This was in use until 1988 when Rolex released the ref. 16520 with an automatic “self-winding” movement. Rolex outsourced this moment, utilizing the Zenith 400 movement, originally manufactured for the “Zenith El-Primero.” For use in the ref. 16520, Rolex required approximately 200 modifications to the Zenith movement, which remained in use for twelve years. As a result, Daytonas from this period are commonly referred to as “Zenith Daytonas.” In this reference, Rolex also incorporated more durable sapphire crystals, helping to increase the depth rating to a guaranteed 100m or 330ft. This incredible two-tone Rolex Daytona ref. 16523 is a true time capsule, remaining in exceptional condition throughout and accompanied by its original boxes, papers, accessories, and original sales receipt. description: The art of collecting military-issued timepieces has never been more interesting or captivating than in today’s day and age. These alluring timepieces have been sought after for as long as collectors have existed, however, due to the availability of archived information we now possess, the community has never been more interconnected or informed. As we collectively continue to discover new information we reinforce our understanding of where, when, and why these incredible timepieces were enlisted. Upon first glance this Omega Seamaster 300 may seem like any other well-preserved reference 165.024 model, however, this unassuming example happens to be a part of one of the most prestigious family of timepieces, those issued by the British Ministry of Defense. Like the Rolex ref. 5517 “MilSub”, which the Omega “MilMaster” actually predates, this watch was created to adhere to the exact specifications set forth by the MOD to fit the necessary military applications it would be used for while also being able to survive the environment of global conflict. Omega created two very similar Seamaster 300 models for the MOD, one for the British Royal Navy, and the other for the British Royal Army which is also designated as the “W10” model. While both of these remain almost exactly the same, both feature military branch-specific engravings on the case back and the British Navy models are also more commonly seen with the iconic circle “T” printing on the dial which designated the use of tritium for the luminous material. Though some “W10” models also featured the circle “T” designation on the dial, most were fitted with standard dials with no military designations. Besides the previously listed differences, both the Navy and Army models feature the iconic sword-shaped hands (which carried over to the Rolex contract), bakelite luminous bezels, fixed strap bars, and the in-house Omega Cal. 552 automatic winding movement. Considering vintage diving watches as a category, the Omega Seamaster 300 has cemented itself as one of the most important watches to come from the “Golden Era” of sports timepieces. The specific aesthetic of the 165.024 evokes a true feeling of adventure and exploration which is all but amplified by the military specifications and provenance. title: PolyWatch Plastic Crystal Polish & Scratch Remover (5g)
description: PolyWatch Plastic Crystal Polish is the trusted solution for restoring scratched acrylic and plastic watch crystals. A favorite among watchmakers, collectors, and enthusiasts, this specialized polishing compound is formulated to remove light scratches, scuffs, and surface marks while restoring clarity and shine to vintage acrylic crystals. Ideal for vintage Rolex, Omega, Tudor, and countless other watches fitted with acrylic crystals, PolyWatch uses an ultra-fine polishing compound that gently smooths the surface of the crystal without the need for replacement. With just a small amount of polish and a microfiber cloth, minor imperfections can often be removed in minutes, bringing tired crystals back to life. How To Use Apply a small amount of PolyWatch to the acrylic crystal. Polish the surface using a clean microfiber cloth with firm, circular motions. Continue polishing until light scratches and scuffs are reduced or eliminated. Specifications Designed for acrylic and plastic watch crystals Removes light scratches, scuffs, and surface marks Restores clarity and original appearance Easy, non-abrasive application 5g tube One tube provides approximately 10–12 applications, depending on crystal size and condition An essential addition to any watch enthusiast's toolkit, PolyWatch offers a fast, affordable way to maintain the appearance of vintage watches and keep their original acrylic crystals looking their best. Please Note: PolyWatch is designed exclusively for acrylic and other plastic watch crystals and should not be used on sapphire or mineral glass crystals . It is most effective at removing light surface scratches, scuffs, and haze. Deep gouges, cracks, or significant damage cannot be repaired with polishing alone and will require professional restoration or crystal replacement.
